n: Amaziah, son of the murdered Joash, becomes king of Judah around 796 BC.
He was twenty-five and reigned twenty-nine years.
He did right, but not with David’s wholeheartedness—following the pattern of his father, good at first but inconsistent.

f.w: yet not like David his father

n: Local shrines continued in use.
Once firmly in power, Amaziah executes the officials who assassinated his father.

f.w: slew his servants which had slain the king his father

n: But he spares their children, obeying the law of Moses: each person answers for his own sin. This was unusual in the ancient world, where whole families were often punished.

f.w: The fathers shall not be put to death for the children

n: He defeats Edom in the Valley of Salt, south of the Dead Sea, and captures Sela, a rock fortress, renaming it Joktheel.

f.g: ‘the rock,’ an Edomite stronghold, perhaps near later Petra.

n: Proud of his victory, Amaziah challenges Jehoash of Israel to battle: “Let us face each other.”

f.w: look one another in the face

n: Jehoash answers with a mocking fable: a thistle asks a cedar for a marriage alliance, and a passing animal tramples it. Judah is the little thistle; Israel the mighty cedar.

f.w: The thistle that was in Lebanon

n: Jehoash’s advice is blunt: you beat Edom and it has gone to your head—enjoy your glory and stay home, or you’ll bring ruin on yourself and Judah.

f.w: thine heart hath lifted thee up

n: Amaziah won’t listen. The armies meet at Beth-shemesh, west of Jerusalem in Judah’s own territory.

f.g: ‘house of the sun,’ a border town in Judah’s lowlands.

n: Judah is routed and its soldiers flee home.
Jehoash captures Amaziah, marches on Jerusalem, and breaks down about 600 feet of the city wall on its northern side.

f.g: a gate on the north side, facing Ephraim.

n: He loots the temple and palace treasures and takes hostages back to Samaria. Pride brought Judah humiliation.

f.g: people held to guarantee good behavior.

n: Jehoash’s other acts are recorded in Israel’s chronicles.
Jehoash dies, and his son Jeroboam II succeeds him.
Amaziah outlived Jehoash by fifteen years.
His other acts are recorded in Judah’s chronicles.
A conspiracy forms in Jerusalem; Amaziah flees to the fortress city of Lachish but is killed there. Chronicles links this to his worship of Edomite gods.

f.g: a major fortified city in Judah’s lowlands.

n: His body is brought back on horses and buried in Jerusalem.
The people crown his sixteen-year-old son Azariah, also called Uzziah.

f.g: ‘Jehovah has helped’; also called Uzziah, ‘Jehovah is my strength.’

n: Azariah rebuilt Elath on the Red Sea, restoring Judah’s access to trade routes.

f.g: a port on the Gulf of Aqaba, near Ezion-geber.

n: Jeroboam II begins a long reign of forty-one years in Israel (about 793–753 BC, including a co-regency).
Spiritually, he too followed Jeroboam I’s calf worship.
Yet politically he restored Israel’s borders from Hamath in the north to the Dead Sea, as the prophet Jonah—the same Jonah sent to Nineveh—had foretold.

f.g: the Dead Sea (the Sea of the Arabah).
a city-state in central Syria; its ‘entrance’ marked Israel’s ideal northern border.

n: The Lord saw how bitterly Israel suffered—with no one left, slave or free, to help them.

f.w: there was not any shut up, nor any left
f.g: an idiom meaning ‘no one at all, bond or free.’

n: Though Israel deserved judgment, the Lord had not yet decreed its end. He saved them through Jeroboam II. This was an age of prosperity, but also of injustice condemned by the prophets Amos and Hosea.

f.w: blot out the name of Israel

n: His military successes included recovering Damascus and Hamath, the old territory of David and Solomon.

f.g: which had once belonged to the united kingdom under David and Solomon.

n: Jeroboam II dies and his son Zachariah succeeds him—the fourth generation of Jehu’s dynasty, as the Lord had promised.
